Seed Conjecture Sources

Where open conjectures exist as human-checked Lean 4 statements, how good each source's checking is, and a per-problem catalog with the metadata needed to decide whether a problem is added to a graph. Feeds F11-Q3 / F11-T5 (the recorded fact pass over the registry).

Research date 2026-09-08 · Registry pin google-deepmind/formal-conjectures@c7f31d5 (2026-09-08) · Toolchain leanprover/lean4:v4.33.1 · Mathlib v4.33.1 (0df444a360eaa60ab8c11dca51a86af692955474)
Catalog: 640 Erdős problems with a Lean file, 335 open on erdosproblems.com, 327 scoreable seed candidates, 23 graded A and 83 graded B · 448 non-Erdős files with open statements · Rebuild with docs/seed_conjecture_sources_build.py

There is one real source. Google DeepMind's formal-conjectures registry holds essentially every reviewed Lean statement of an open problem. Everything else either vendors its statements from there or is unreviewed AI output.

Its checking is good enough to inherit from, not good enough to skip review. Every statement gets human review, but by one approver, with no per-statement record and no "verified" tier. The registry has itself corrected 291 misformalizations, about 11% of its statements, most of them found by provers rather than reviewers.

A filtered subset gets you what you actually want. Statements that Thomas Bloom selected for FrontierMath Erdős, that survived AlphaProof Nexus and Aletheia's prover and literature sweeps, and that use only Mathlib definitions, carry enough external evidence to meet D-9's top grade on its operational definition. The remaining cost per target is one non-author back-translation, which you can do yourself with tooling in well under an hour. The catalog below applies that filter to every formalized Erdős problem.

1. The grading scale

D-9 makes fidelity a graded status, not a yes/no. The grades, low to high, with the floor below which no proving compute is allocated:

mechanical-onlyback-translatedauthor-attestedexpert-attestedpublished-and-uncontested

The top grade is operational, not reputational: N days public in a D-10 venue, M independent proof attempts, zero confirmed defect claims. Pilot defaults are N = 30 and M = 3. That definition is the lever in this report, because the registry's public history already supplies both N and M for many statements.

3. How Formal Conjectures actually checks a statement

Verified from the repository's CONTRIBUTING.md, AGENTS.md, CI workflows, review records and the May 2026 paper (arXiv 2605.13171).

Intake

Anyone with a Google CLA submits. Every statement carries exactly one @[category research open | research solved | textbook | API | test], at least one @[AMS n], and a module docstring citing the source. Questions are written with answer(sorry). AGENTS.md adds a Source Fidelity rule: match quantifier order, bounds and hypotheses; test edge cases.

Mechanical checks

lake --wfail build and test, a category-contradiction script, copyright headers, and custom linters: ExistsImplicationLinter (catches the classic ∃ x, P x → Q bug), StubLinter (no sorry in definitions, no new axioms), metadata linters. There is no triviality or vacuity check in CI.

Human review

The paper says every contribution gets review by someone with Lean and domain expertise. In practice the two most recent merged PRs each had one approval, by the lead maintainer. No CODEOWNERS file, no per-statement reviewer record, no "verified" label. Fixed statements do not retain a record of the old, wrong version.

Adversarial provers

The strongest check, and it runs outside CI: AlphaProof, Gemini and Aristotle are pointed at the registry, and "manually inspecting these results primarily reveals misformalizations." Nearly every incident in §5 was caught this way.

Link to erdosproblems.com

Mechanical in both directions. A push to the registry auto-updates the site's "Formalised statement? Yes" link, which points at main, not a commit. The site records no formalization-verified status and Bloom does not review the Lean, except the 18 Epoch statements.

Measured defect rate

291 misformalizations corrected up to the frozen bench-v1 tag of 2,615 statements. By class: misrepresentation (quantifiers, connectives, missing hypotheses) 48%, semantic (types, operators) 35%, implicit conventions 8%, reporting 5%, syntactic 3%, genuine mathematical error 0.3%.

Every human-reviewed Lean benchmark keeps shedding statement errors after release. These numbers set the prior for any statement you inherit.

The Aletheia row is the one that matters for an open-problem network. When the statement admits a weak reading, a prover finds the weak reading. Lean cannot see that. That is the residual risk D-9 already names as permanent, and it is why "no human reviewer" cannot mean "no non-author ever reads the statement".

5. What review misses on open problems

Concrete cases, all from the Erdős subset, grouped by the defect class. Each of these is a wording pattern the catalog screens for.

  • Source ambiguity. #728 had "a number of trivial solutions to the problem as written"; the community reconstructed the intended statement on the forum before a Lean proof meant anything. #1026 was ambiguous from 1975. #124 has two readings of P(d,0) versus P(d,1).
  • Source error. #75: Erdős dropped an ℵ₁-vertices condition in one of his own papers; Aletheia proved the flawed version correctly. The curator cannot catch this, which is why author-attested is non-terminal in D-9.
  • Density. "Positive density" and "natural density" were formalized three different ways in #125, #741 and #424; AlphaProof exploited natural density before the statements were amended to lower or upper density. The #424 reporter asked for an audit of every "positive density" problem, which is still open.
  • Asymptotic notation. #394 had the sides of ≫ swapped for months; #728's n + O(log n) was the whole disagreement.
  • Junk values and guards. #480 said m ≠ 0 where it needed n ≠ 0; Aristotle proved it at n = 0 through Mathlib's 1/0 = 0. Bateman–Horn's tprod had the same shape in 2026.
  • Missing hypothesis. #859 lacked t ≥ 1; #56 lacked a constraint and fell to counterexamples "with tiny parameters like 2".
  • Definition mismatch. #918 used subgraph where induced subgraph was meant, found only when AlphaProof produced trivial solutions.

6. The seed filter, and how the trust score encodes it

A recorded fact pass over the registry, as F11-Q3 asks for. The catalog in §9 computes a heuristic trust score per problem from exactly these predicates; the "why" cell on each row lists which fired. The score is a triage aid derived from this report, not a certificate. D-9 certificates are still recorded per target by the fidelity command.

  1. Pin the registry. Import at an immutable tag or dated commit, never from main. The catalog is built at c7f31d5; record the commit in provenance.
  2. Erdős, research open, in an included domain. AMS 11 (number theory) or 05 (combinatorics), matching the protocol's target domains. Rows with no open Lean statement or a closed site status score n/a.
  3. Bloom-selected (+2, +1 more if the FC statement was vendored and asserted open at Epoch's pin). The problem is one of the 70 Bloom chose for FrontierMath Erdős. This is the only curated "significant and difficult" list that exists, made by the person who maintains the informal side.
  4. Survived the sweeps (+2). The statement was among the 353 AlphaProof Nexus attempted (Feb 2026) and is still open. This is evidence against trivial-reading defects. Aletheia's Dec 2025 literature search covered all 700 then-open problems, so "still open" also carries that check against a solution already in the literature.
  5. No misformalization issue (+1 if none ever; −2 if one is open). A closed one is neutral because the fixed version is what survived.
  6. Public long enough (+1 if the Lean file is 180+ days old; −1 if it changed in the last 30 days). This is D-9's N, read off the registry's history.
  7. Mathlib definitions only (+1). A file-local definition is a second review object under D-9 and the #918 failure mode.
  8. Wording hazards (−1 each, max −2): density, "sufficiently large", asymptotic notation, cardinal conditions, "almost all". These are the classes in §5.
  9. Value-typed (−1). A main statement of the form … = answer(sorry) is a question, not a conjecture; Epoch excluded these too.
  10. Site status lag (−2). The AI wiki records a full solution while the site still says open.

Letters: A at 6 or more points, B at 4–5, C at 2–3, D below. Expect the A rows to be the Stage 0 shortlist; F11's default is five.

Then certify, cheaply

For each shortlisted problem, the D-9 mechanizable pass and one human act:

  • Triviality control: try to prove the statement and its negation with Lean automation and a short agent run. A cheap proof of either is a defect, not a result.
  • Two or three consequence or special-case lemmas from the informal statement, checked against the Lean.
  • Back-translation: an LLM informalizes the Lean without seeing the source; a non-author compares it to the erdosproblems.com wording. Compile-plus-two-judge agreement with human majority runs near 90% in the literature, so this is a screen, and the non-author's read is the certificate.
  • Record the external history as the published-and-uncontested evidence: days public in the registry, the named prover attempts, zero confirmed defects.

Decision for Mike D-9 says M independent proof attempts are earned "in public venues, not in-network". Counting AlphaProof Nexus, Aletheia and Aristotle runs on the registry as those attempts is consistent with that wording and is what makes the top grade reachable without an in-network expert. If you count them, the seeds enter at published-and-uncontested after a back-translation you can do yourself. If you do not, they enter at back-translated and stay there until three network provers have tried. Either way the floor for allocating compute is met.

7. What "no human reviewer" can honestly mean

It can mean no external expert, no hire, and no per-artifact approval click. It cannot mean nobody reads the statement, for two reasons the evidence forces. First, the dominant defect on open problems is an unintended reading of an ambiguous source, which no kernel and no lint can detect; a non-author back-translation is the cheapest known detector. Second, the registry you are inheriting from has no per-statement review record, so its own review cannot be cited as yours. The filter shrinks the human step to a comparison of two paragraphs per target.

8. Licensing

  • Formal Conjectures: code Apache-2.0, prose CC-BY 4.0, third-party content under its own license. Inheriting statements with attribution and the pinned commit is explicitly intended; Epoch already does it.
  • erdosproblems.com: no license text anywhere on the site. It asks for the citation form "T. F. Bloom, Erdős Problem #N, https://www.erdosproblems.com/N, accessed date". The catalog below quotes each problem's statement for decision-making with that citation implied by the link; a target record should cite rather than copy, and cite Erdős's original papers as the site asks.
  • teorth/erdosproblems (the status database) and alphaproof-nexus-results: Apache-2.0. Epoch's LeanOpenProblems: MIT for scripts, Apache-2.0 for vendored statements. The AI wiki is CC-BY-SA via GitHub wiki defaults; rows are quoted as data.

9. Catalog: every Erdős problem with a Lean statement

One row per file in FormalConjectures/ErdosProblems/ at the pinned commit. Columns and where each comes from:

  • #, prize: erdosproblems.com problem number (linked) and Erdős's prize as shown on the site.
  • Site status: the label on the site (OPEN, PROVED (LEAN), DISPROVED, …) with its explanatory line, the status database's last-update date, and the page's last-edited date. Open here means "Bloom is personally unaware of a solution".
  • Informal conjecture: the site's statement verbatim (LaTeX rendered); the expandable list gives every Lean declaration in the file with its category, AMS codes, docstring and any proof link.
  • Area: AMS codes from the Lean attributes, then the site's tags.
  • Standing since: earliest year among the site's citation keys, so "1974 (52 yr)" means the oldest source Bloom cites is from 1974. The first four keys are shown.
  • Lean: the file at the pinned commit, the main open statement's name, when the file was added to the registry, its last change, its commit count, and any file-local definitions. Toolchain and Mathlib for every row are the pin in the header.
  • Proof (closed problems): Lean proof links from formal_proof attributes on solved statements, and the solved statement's docstring, which names the informal proof and its reference.
  • Benchmarks: FrontierMath Erdős membership (FC-reviewed 48, autoformalized 17, or Bloom-selected but excluded as estimate-type), Bloom's top-10 list, and AlphaProof Nexus (attempted count, or the solved statement names).
  • Misformalization: every issue or PR in the registry labelled misformalization that names this problem, with state and dates.
  • AI wiki: rows from the Erdős-problems AI wiki (frozen 2026-06-30) for this problem, with section, systems, date and outcome.
  • Trust: the §6 score and its reasons.

Pages the scrape could not fetch (rows fall back to the Lean docstring and the status database): none.

 Is there some $k$ such that every large integer is the sum of a prime and at most $k$ powers of 2?
6 Lean statements: 3 research open, 3 research solved
  • erdos_10 research open AMS 5 AMS 11
    Is there some $k$ such that every integer is the sum of a prime and at most $k$ powers of $2$?
  • erdos_10.variants.gallagher research solved AMS 5 AMS 11
    Gallagher [Ga75] has shown that for any $ϵ > 0$ there exists $k(ϵ)$ such that the set of integers which are the sum of a prime and at most $k(ϵ)$ many powers of $2$ has lower density at least $1 - ϵ$. Ref: Gallagher, P. X., _Primes and powers of 2_.
  • erdos_10.variants.granville_soundararajan_odd research open AMS 5 AMS 11
    Granville and Soundararajan [GrSo98] have conjectured that at most $3$ powers of $2$ suffice for all odd integers, and hence at most $4$ powers of $2$ suffice for all even integers. Ref: Granville, A. and Soundararajan, K., _A Binary Additive Problem of Erdős and the Order of $2$ mod $p^2$_
  • erdos_10.variants.grechuk_example research solved AMS 5 AMS 11
    Bogdan Grechuk has observed that `1117175146` is not the sum of a prime and at most $3$ powers of $2$.
  • erdos_10.variants.two_pows research solved AMS 5 AMS 11
    There are infinitely many even integers not the sum of a prime and $2$ powers of $2$
  • erdos_10.variants.grechuk research open AMS 5 AMS 11
    Bogdan Grechuk has observed that $1117175146$ is not the sum of a prime and at most $3$ powers of $2$, and pointed out that parity considerations, coupled with the fact that there are many integers not the sum of a prime and $2$ powers of $2$ suggest that there exist infinitely many even integers which are not the sum of a prime and at most $3$ powers of $2$).

 Let $A=\{n_1<n_2<\cdots\}$ be an infinite sequence of integers, and let $\phi_A(k)$ count the number of $1\leq m\leq n_k$ such that the fraction $\frac{m}{n_k}$ does not have denominator $n_j$ for $j<k$ when written in lowest form; equivalently,\[\frac{n_k}{(m,n_k)}\neq n_j\]for all $1\leq j<k$.Is there a sequence $A$ such that\[\lim_{N\to \infty}\frac{1}{N}\sum_{k\leq N}\frac{\phi_A(k)}{n_k}=0?\]
5 Lean statements: 5 research solved
  • erdos_1000 research solved AMS 11 · Lean proof
    Let $A=\{n_1<n_2<\cdots\}$ be an infinite sequence of integers, and let $\phi_A(k)$ count the number of $1\leq m\leq n_k$ such that the fraction $\frac{m}{n_k}$ does not have denominator $n_j$ for $j<k$ when written in lowest form; equivalently, $$ \frac{n_k}{(m,n_k)}\neq n_j $$ for all $1\leq j<k$. Is there a sequence $A$ such that $$ \lim_{N\to \infty}\frac{1}{N}\sum_{k\leq N}\frac{\phi_A(k)}{n_k}=0? $$ This was solved by Haight [Ha] who proved that such a sequence does exist (contrary to Erdős' expectations).
  • erdos_1000.variants.totient_le research solved AMS 11
    It is trivial that $\phi_A(k)\geq \phi(n_k)$, where $\phi$ is the Euler totient function.
  • erdos_1000.variants.liminf_eq_zero research solved AMS 11
    The study of $\phi_A$ was introduced by Cassels [Ca50b], who proved that there exist sequences such that $$ \liminf_{N\to \infty}\frac{1}{N}\sum_{k\leq N}\frac{\phi_A(k)}{n_k}=0. $$
  • erdos_1000.variants.not_tendsto_zero research solved AMS 11
    Erdős [Er64b] proved that the limit of $\frac{\phi_A(k)}{n_k}$ as $k\to \infty$ cannot be $0$.
  • erdos_1000.variants.limsup_eq_one research solved AMS 11
    In fact he proved that if $\liminf \frac{\phi_A(k)}{n_k}=0$ then $\limsup \frac{\phi_A(k)}{n_k}=1$.

2 Lean statements: 1 research open, 1 research solved

    For any $0<\alpha<1$, let $f(\alpha,n)=\frac{1}{\log n}\sum_{1\leq k\leq n}(\tfrac{1}{2}- \{ \alpha k\})$. Does $f(\alpha,n)$ have an asymptotic distribution function? In other words, is there a non-decreasing function $g$ such that $g(-\infty)=0$, $g(\infty)=1$, and $\lim_{n\to \infty}\lvert \{ \alpha\in (0,1): f(\alpha,n)\leq c\}\rvert=g(c)$?
  • erdos_1002.variants.kesten research solved AMS 11
    Kesten [Ke60] proved that if $f(\alpha,\beta,n)=\frac{1}{\log n}\sum_{1\leq k\leq n}(\tfrac{1}{2}- \{\beta+\alpha k\})$ then $f(\alpha,\beta,n)$ has asymptotic distribution function $g(c)=\frac{1}{\pi}\int_{-\infty}^{\rho c}\frac{1}{1+t^2}\mathrm{d}t$, where $\rho>0$ is an explicit constant.

    The dimension of a graph $G$ is the minimal $n$ such that $G$ can be embedded in $\mathbb{R}^n$ such that every edge of $G$ is a unit line segment. What is the smallest number of edges in a graph with dimension $4$? Answer: The smallest number of edges is $9$, achieved solely by $K_{3,3}$, proved by House [Ho13]. An alternative proof was given by Chaffee and Noble [ChNo16], who also prove that the smallest number of edges in a graph of dimension $5$ is $15$ (achieved by $K_6$ and $K_{1,3,3}$).

This is false, and $c_t<2$ for all $t$: a counterexample is provided by Wood [Wo13b], who constructs, for any $r\geq 2$, a triangle-free $2$-degenerate $r$-uniform hypergraph with chromatic number $3$. This stronger conjecture appears to have been first proved by Tidor, Wang, and Yang [TWY16], and is also implicit in work of Wagner [Wa17]. 4 Lean statements: 4 research solved
  • erdos_1034 research solved AMS 5 · Lean proof
    Let $G$ be a graph on $n$ vertices with $>n^2/4$ many edges. Must there be a triangle $T$ in $G$ and vertices $y_1,\ldots,y_t$, where $t>(\frac{1}{2}-o(1))n$, such that every $y_i$ is joined to at least two vertices of $T$? A conjecture of Erdős and Faudree; a stronger version of [905]. This has been solved in the negative by Ma and Tang [MaTa25], who construct a graph with $n$ vertices and $>n^2/4$ edges in which every triangle has at most $(2-(5/2)^{1/2}+o(1))n$ vertices adjacent to at least two of its vertices (note that $2-(5/2)^{1/2}\approx 0.4189$).
  • erdos_1034.variants.lower_bound research solved AMS 5
    Erdős and Faudree asked about the threshold $h(n)$ such that every graph with $n$ vertices and $>n^2/4$ edges contained a triangle and $h(n)$ other vertices which are connected to at least two vertices of the triangle.  Let $f\in \mathbb{C}[x]$ be a monic polynomial with $m$ distinct roots, and let $c>0$ be a constant small enough such that $\{ z: \lvert f(z)\rvert\leq c\}$ has $m$ distinct connected components.Must all these components be convex?
6 Lean statements: 1 research open, 5 research solved
  • erdos_1047 research solved AMS 30 AMS 52 · Lean proof
    Let $f\in \mathbb{C}[x]$ be a monic polynomial with $m$ distinct roots, and let $c>0$ be a constant small enough such that $\{ z: \lvert f(z)\rvert\leq c\}$ has $m$ distinct connected components. Must all these components be convex? A question of Grunsky, which was reported by Erdős, Herzog, and Piranian [EHP58]. The answer is no, as shown by Pommerenke [Po61], who showed that, if $k$ is sufficiently large, and $f(z)=z^k(z-a)$ where $a$ is sufficiently close to $(1+\frac{1}{k})k^{\frac{1}{k+1}}$, then $\{ z: \lvert f(z)\rvert\leq 1\}$ has two components, and the component which contains $0$ is not convex. This was formalized in Lean by Alexeev using Aristotle.
  • erdos_1047.variants.pommerenke research solved AMS 30 AMS 52
    The answer is no, as shown by Pommerenke [Po61], who showed that, if $k$ is sufficiently large, and $f(z)=z^k(z-a)$ where $a$ is sufficiently close to $(1+\frac{1}{k})k^{\frac{1}{k+1}}$, then $\{ z: \lvert f(z)\rvert\leq 1\}$ has two components, and the component which contains $0$ is not convex.
  • erdos_1047.variants.goodman research solved AMS 30 AMS 52

    If $f\in \mathbb{C}[x]$ is a monic polynomial with all roots satisfying $\lvert z\rvert \leq r$ for some $r<2$, then must $$\{ z: \lvert f(z)\rvert <1\}$$ have a connected component with diameter $>2-r$?  Is\[\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{2^n-3}\]irrational?
4 Lean statements: 1 research open, 3 research solved
  • erdos_1050 research solved AMS 11 · Lean proof
    **Erdős Problem 1050.** The series $\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{2^n - 3}$ is irrational. The source sum runs over $n \ge 1$; as a `tsum` over `ℕ` (which starts at $0$) it is reindexed $n \mapsto n + 1$, i.e. $\sum_{n=0}^\infty 1/(2^{n+1} - 3)$.
  • erdos_1050.variants.two_pow_sub_one research solved AMS 11 · Lean proof
    **Erdős Problem 1050, variant [Er48].** Erdős proved that the related series $\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{2^n - 1}$ (which equals the Lambert series $\sum_n \frac{\tau(n)}{2^n}$, where $\tau$ is the divisor function) is irrational. This is the $q = 2$, $r = -1$ case of Borwein's general theorem `Erdos1050.erdos_1050.variants.borwein` below.
  • erdos_1050.variants.borwein research solved AMS 11 · Lean proof
    **Erdős Problem 1050, variant [Bo91].** Borwein's general theorem: for every integer $q \ge 2$ and rational $r \ne 0$ with $r \ne -q^n$ for all $n \ge 1$, the series $\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{q^n + r}$ is irrational. Problem 1050 is the case $q = 2$, $r = -3$; the [Er48] variant is $q = 2$, $r = -1$.
  • erdos_1050.variants.transcendental research open AMS 11
    **Erdős Problem 1050, variant [Er88c] (open).** Erdős conjectured that $\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{2^n + t}$ is *transcendental* for every integer $t \ne 0$ — strictly stronger than the irrationality established by Borwein [Bo91]. This remains open. Two exclusions make the series well-posed and the claim non-vacuous, exactly as in Borwein's theorem: $t \ne -2^n$ for all $n \ge 1$ (so no denominator vanishes), and $t \ne 0$ (at $t = 0$ the series is the rational $\sum_{n \ge 1} 2^{-n} = 1$, hence not transcendental).

6 Lean statements: 1 research open, 5 research solved
  • erdos_1063.better_upper research open AMS 11 · value-typed
    Estimate $n_k$ by finding a better upper bound than Cambie's $n_k \leq k \cdot \operatorname{lcm}(1, \dotsc, k-1)$. The comparator takes its least common multiple in `ℕ` and casts the result. Writing the ascription as `((… ).lcm (fun n : ℕ => n) : ℝ)` instead puts it on the `Finset.lcm` application, so the coercion lands on `n` and the `lcm` is taken in `ℝ`, where `lcm` of non-zero elements is `1` and the whole comparator collapses to `k`.
  • erdos_1063.variants.exists_exception research solved AMS 11
    Erdős and Selfridge noted that, for $n \ge 2k$ with $k \ge 2$, at least one of the numbers $n - i$ for $0 \le i < k$ fails to divide $\binom{n}{k}$ ([ErSe83]).
  • erdos_1063.variants.small_values research solved AMS 11
    The initial values satisfy $n_2 = 4$, $n_3 = 6$, $n_4 = 9$, and $n_5 = 12$ ([Gu04], Problem B31).
  • erdos_1063.variants.monier_upper_bound research solved AMS 11
    Monier observed that $n_k \le k!$ for $k \ge 3$ ([Mo85]), since $\binom{k!}{k}$ is divisible by $k! - i$ for $1 \le i < k$. The hypothesis `3 ≤ k` is necessary. At $k = 2$ the bound is false: $n_2 = 4$ and $2! = 2$.
  • erdos_1063.variants.cambie_upper_bound research solved AMS 11
    [Cambie observed](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1063) the improved bound $n_k \le k \cdot \operatorname{lcm}(1, \dotsc, k - 1)$. The hypothesis `3 ≤ k` is necessary here too. At $k = 2$ the right hand side is $2 \cdot \operatorname{lcm}(1) = 2$, while $n_2 = 4$. The source writes the bound as $k[2, 3, \dotsc, k-1]$. That agrees with the range used here, because including $1$ does not change a least common multiple.
  • erdos_1063.variants.exp_upper_bound research solved AMS 11
    The least common multiple bound implies $n_k \le \exp((1 + o(1))k)$.

 We say that $A\subseteq \mathbb{N}$ has property $P$ if, for all $n\geq 1$, there are only finitely many $a\in A$ such that $n+a$ is squarefree.We say that $A$ has property $Q$ if there are infinitely many $n$ such that $n+a$ is squarefree for all $a<n$. How fast must sequences $A=\{a_1<a_2<\cdots\}$ with properties $P$ or $Q$ increase?
4 Lean statements: 4 research solved
  • erdos_1102.density_zero_of_P research solved AMS 11 · Lean proof
    If `A = {a₁ < a₂ < …}` has property P, then `A` has natural density `0`. Equivalently, `(a_j / j) → ∞` as `j → ∞`. -
  • erdos_1102.exists_sequence_with_P research solved AMS 11 · Lean proof
    Conversely, for any function `f : ℕ → ℕ` that goes to infinity, there exists a strictly increasing sequence `A = {a₁ < a₂ < …}` with property P such that `(a_j / j) ≤ f(j)` for all `j`. -
  • erdos_1102.upper_density_Q research solved AMS 11 · Lean proof
    Every sequence with property Q has upper density at most `6 / π^2`. -
  • erdos_1102.lower_density_Q_exists research solved AMS 11 · Lean proof
    There exists an infinite sequence $A = {a₁ < a₂ < …} ⊂ \mathsf{SF}$ where $\mathsf{SF} := \mathbb{N} \setminus \bigcup_{p} p^{2}\mathbb{N}$, i.e. the set of squarefree numbers. The set `A` has property `Q` and natural density `6 / π^2`. Equivalently, `(j / a_j) → 6/π^2` as `j → ∞`. -

  • erdos_1119 research solved AMS 3 AMS 30
    Let $\mathfrak{m}$ be an infinite cardinal with $\aleph_0 < \mathfrak{m} < \mathfrak{c} = 2^{\aleph_0}$. Let $\{f_\alpha\}$ be a family of entire functions such that, for every $z_0 \in \mathbb{C}$, there are at most $\mathfrak{m}$ distinct values of $f_\alpha(z_0)$. Must $\{f_\alpha\}$ have cardinality at most $\mathfrak{m}$? This is Problem 2.46 in [Ha74], where it is attributed to Erdős. The question is **independent of ZFC**, so the headline statement carries `answer(sorry)`: it is neither provable nor refutable from the usual axioms of set theory. The answer is yes if $\mathfrak{m}^+ < \mathfrak{c}$ (see `erdos_1119.variants.easy_case`), so the question reduces to the case $\mathfrak{m…
  • erdos_1119.variants.easy_case research solved AMS 3 AMS 30
    The 'easy' case of Erdős Problem 1119: if moreover $\mathfrak{m}^+ < \mathfrak{c}$, then any family of entire functions taking at most $\mathfrak{m}$ distinct values at each point has cardinality at most $\mathfrak{m}$. In [Ha74] it is written that this is 'easy to see'.
  • erdos_1119.variants.erdos_wetzel research solved AMS 3 AMS 30
    Erdős's theorem [Er64g], answering a question of Wetzel: if $\mathfrak{c} > \aleph_1$, then every family of entire functions taking only countably many distinct values at each point $z_0 \in \mathbb{C}$ is itself countable.
  • erdos_1119.variants.erdos_wetzel_ch research solved AMS 3 AMS 30
    Erdős [Er64g] also showed that the previous statement fails under the continuum hypothesis: if $\mathfrak{c} = \aleph_1$, then there is an **uncountable** family of entire functions taking only countably many distinct values at each point $z_0 \in \mathbb{C}$.
  • erdos_1119.test.empty_family test AMS 3 AMS 30
    Sanity check: the empty family of entire functions satisfies both the value-bound hypothesis and the cardinality conclusion of `erdos_1119`, for any infinite $\mathfrak{m}$.

 If $C_1,\ldots,C_n$ are circles in $\mathbb{R}^2$ with radii $r_1,\ldots,r_n$ such that no line disjoint from all the circles divides them into two non-empty sets then the circles can be covered by a circle of radius $r=\sum r_i$.
2 Lean statements: 2 research solved
  • erdos_1121 research solved AMS 52 · Lean proof
    If $C_1,\ldots,C_n$ are circles in $\mathbb{R}^2$ with radii $r_1,\ldots,r_n$ such that no line disjoint from all the circles divides them into two non-empty sets then the circles can be covered by a circle of radius $r=\sum r_i$. This is true, and was proved by Goodman and Goodman [GoGo45] (whose proof also generalises to higher dimensions). A generalisation to convex bodies was proved by Hadwiger [Ha47]. An alternative proof is given by Bezdek and Litvak [BeLi16].
  • erdos_1121.variants.higher_dimension research solved AMS 52
    The proof of Goodman and Goodman [GoGo45] also generalises to higher dimensions: if $B_1,\ldots,B_n$ are balls in $\mathbb{R}^d$ with radii $r_1,\ldots,r_n$ such that no hyperplane disjoint from all the balls divides them into two non-empty sets then the balls can be covered by a ball of radius $r=\sum r_i$.

4 Lean statements: 4 research solved
  • erdos_1128.prikryMills research solved AMS 3 AMS 5
    **Prikry–Mills counterexample** (key lemma): There exists a 2-colouring $f$ of a set of cardinality $\aleph_1$ cubed such that no countable box $A_1 \times B_1 \times C_1$ is monochromatic. This is the unpublished result of Prikry and Mills (1978). The proof proceeds by transfinite induction along $\omega_1$, which has uncountable cofinality, ensuring every countable box is non-monochromatic.
  • erdos_1128 research solved AMS 3 AMS 5
    **Erdős Problem 1128** (disproved by Prikry–Mills, 1978): Erdős asked whether every 2-colouring of $A \times B \times C$, where $|A| = |B| = |C| = \aleph_1$, must contain a monochromatic countable box $A_1 \times B_1 \times C_1$ with $|A_1| = |B_1| = |C_1| = \aleph_0$. The answer is **No**: Prikry and Mills constructed a 2-colouring of $\omega_1^3$ with no monochromatic countable box. Note: The positive statement asserts that every 2-colouring of every $\aleph_1^3$ contains a monochromatic countably infinite box. Since the answer is False, this positive statement fails.
  • erdos_1128.variants.prikryMills_explicit research solved AMS 3 AMS 5
    **Explicit form of Prikry–Mills**: There exists a 2-colouring of $\omega_1 \times \omega_1 \times \omega_1$ such that for every countably infinite $A_1, B_1, C_1 \subseteq \omega_1$, the box $A_1 \times B_1 \times C_1$ is not monochromatic. This is the content of the Prikry–Mills theorem (1978, unpublished), stated using Lean's ordinal type `{o : Ordinal // o < ω_ 1}` as the representation of $\omega_1$.
  • erdos_1128.variants.two_dimensional_false research solved AMS 3 AMS 5
    The claim that every 2-colouring of $\omega_1 \times \omega_1$ has an uncountable monochromatic product rectangle is **false** in ZFC. **Counterexample:** The ordering colouring $f(\alpha, \beta) = 0$ iff $\alpha < \beta$ has no uncountable monochromatic product rectangle $A_1 \times B_1$. **Proof:** If $A_1 \times B_1$ were monochromatic with colour 0, then every element of $A_1$ would be strictly less than every element of $B_1$, making $A_1$ bounded above in $\omega_1$; but any bounded subset of $\omega_1$ is countable (since initial segments are countable), contradicting $A_1$ being uncountable. The colour-1 case is symmetric with the roles of $A_1$ and $B_1$ swapped. Note: The correct…

 Does there exist $A\subset \mathbb{N}$ with lower density $>1/3$ such that $a+b\neq 2^k$ for any $a,b\in A$ and $k\geq 0$?
4 Lean statements: 4 research solved
  • erdos_1136 research solved AMS 11 · Lean proof
    Does there exist $A\subset \mathbb{N}$ with lower density $>1/3$ such that $a+b\neq 2^k$ for any $a,b\in A$ and $k\geq 0$? Müller [Mu11] settled this question in the affirmative: in fact one can take $A$ to be the set of all integers congruent to $3\cdot 2^i\pmod{2^{i+2}}$ for any $i\geq 0$, which has density $1/2$.
  • erdos_1136.variants.multiples_of_three research solved AMS 11
    Achieving density $1/3$ is trivial, taking $A$ to be all multiples of $3$.

  • erdos_1136.variants.upper_bound research solved AMS 11

 Are there infinitely many $n$ such that $n-k^2$ is prime for all $k$ with $(n,k)=1$ and $k^2<n$?
3 Lean statements: 3 research solved
  • erdos_1141.variants.pollack_1_3 research solved AMS 11
    **Theorem 1.3 of [Po17]**: for a quadratic character to a large enough modulus, the primes below $m^{1/4+\varepsilon}$ on which the character is $1$ outnumber any fixed power of $\log m$.
  • erdos_1141.variants.mertens_third research solved AMS 11
    **Mertens' third theorem** [Me1874], in the weakened form the linked proof assumes: the product over the primes up to $n$ of $1 - 1/p$ is at least $1/(3\log n)$. The true asymptotic is $e^{-\gamma}/\log n$, and $e^{-\gamma} > 1/3$, so this bound is weaker than the theorem and is what the deduction needs.
  • erdos_1141 research solved AMS 11 · Lean proof
    Are there infinitely many $n$ such that $n-k^2$ is prime for all $k$ with $(n,k)=1$ and $k^2 < n$? In [Va99] it is asked whether $968$ is the largest integer with this property, but this is an error, since for example $968-9=7\cdot 137$. The list of $n$ satisfying the given property is [A214583] in the OEIS. The largest known such $n$ is $1722$. The answer is negative: [APSSV26b] proves a stronger finiteness theorem, deducing it from Pollack [Po17]. Oriike [Or26] formalised the deduction in Lean. The linked proof is the deduction and not the whole result. It declares Theorem 1.3 of [Po17] and Mertens' third theorem as axioms, so it is marked `conditional` and names both.

  • erdos_1142.variants.mientka_weitzenkamp research solved AMS 11
    Mientka and Weitzenkamp [MiWe69] proved that the only $n \leq 2^{44}$ such that $n > 2$ and $n - 2^k$ is prime for all $k \geq 1$ with $2^k < n$ are $4, 7, 15, 21, 45, 75, 105$.
  • erdos_1142.test_4 test AMS 11
    $4$ satisfies the Erdős 1142 property: $4 - 2 = 2$ is prime.
  • erdos_1142.test_7 test AMS 11
    $7$ satisfies the Erdős 1142 property: $7 - 2 = 5$ and $7 - 4 = 3$ are prime.
  • erdos_1142.test_15 test AMS 11
    $15$ satisfies the Erdős 1142 property: $15 - 2 = 13$, $15 - 4 = 11$, $15 - 8 = 7$.
  • erdos_1142.test_21 test AMS 11
    $21$ satisfies the Erdős 1142 property: $21 - 2 = 19$, $21 - 4 = 17$, $21 - 8 = 13$, $21 - 16 = 5$.
  • erdos_1142.test_45 test AMS 11
    $45$ satisfies the Erdős 1142 property: $45 - 2 = 43$, $45 - 4 = 41$, $45 - 8 = 37$, $45 - 16 = 29$, $45 - 32 = 13$.
  • erdos_1142.test_75 test AMS 11
    $75$ satisfies the Erdős 1142 property: $75 - 2 = 73$, $75 - 4 = 71$, $75 - 8 = 67$, $75 - 16 = 59$, $75 - 32 = 43$, $75 - 64 = 11$.
  • erdos_1142.test_105 test AMS 11
    $105$ satisfies the Erdős 1142 property: the largest known example. $105 - 2 = 103$, $105 - 4 = 101$, $105 - 8 = 97$, $105 - 16 = 89$, $105 - 32 = 73$, $105 - 64 = 41$.
  • erdos_1142.test_not_106 test AMS 11
    $106$ does not satisfy the Erdős 1142 property ($106 - 2 = 104 = 8 \times 13$).

2 Lean statements: 1 research open, 1 textbook
  • erdos_1150 research open AMS 12 AMS 30
    Is there some constant $c > 0$ such that, for all large enough $n$ and all polynomials $P$ of degree $n$ with coefficients in $\{-1, 1\}$, $$\max_{|z|=1} |P(z)| > (1 + c) \sqrt{n}?$$
  • erdos_1150.variants.parseval_lower_bound textbook AMS 12 AMS 30
    The trivial lower bound from Parseval's identity: for any polynomial $P$ of degree $n$ with coefficients in $\{-1, 1\}$, we have $\max_{|z|=1} |P(z)| \geq \sqrt{n+1}$. This follows from Parseval's identity: $$\frac{1}{2\pi} \int_0^{2\pi} |P(e^{i\theta})|^2 d\theta = \sum_{k=0}^{n} |a_k|^2 = n+1$$ since each $|a_k|^2 = 1$. The circle average is bounded by the pointwise supremum squared, so $\max_{|z|=1} |P(z)|^2 \ge n+1$, whence $\max_{|z|=1} |P(z)| \ge \sqrt{n+1}$.

 Let $r\geq 2$ be finite and $\lambda$ be an infinite cardinal. Let $\kappa_\alpha$ be cardinals for all $\alpha<\gamma$. Is it true that\[2^\lambda \to (\kappa_\alpha+1)_{\alpha<\gamma}^{r+1}\]implies\[\lambda \to (\kappa_\alpha)_{\alpha<\gamma}^{r}?\]Here $+$ means cardinal addition, so that $\kappa_\alpha+1=\kappa_\alpha$ if $\kappa_\alpha$ is infinite.
8 Lean statements: 1 API, 5 research open, 2 test
  • erdos_1167 research open AMS 5
    **Erdős Problem 1167.** Let $r \geq 2$ be finite, $\gamma \geq 2$, and $\lambda$ be an infinite cardinal. Let $\kappa_\alpha$ be cardinals for all $\alpha < \gamma$. Is it true that $$2^\lambda \to (\kappa_\alpha + 1)_{\alpha < \gamma}^{r+1}$$ implies $$\lambda \to (\kappa_\alpha)_{\alpha < \gamma}^r?$$ Here $+$ means cardinal addition, so that $\kappa_\alpha + 1 = \kappa_\alpha$ if $\kappa_\alpha$ is infinite. A problem of Erdős, Hajnal, and Rado.
  • finite_targets research open AMS 5
    **Finite-target case.** When all $\kappa_\alpha$ are finite, $\kappa_\alpha + 1$ is the ordinary natural-number successor. Special case of `erdos_1167`.
  • binary_colors research open AMS 5
    **Binary-color case.** The $\gamma = 2$ specialization (two color classes).
  • infinite_targets research open AMS 5
    **Infinite-target case.** When all $\kappa_\alpha \geq \aleph_0$ are infinite and bounded by $\lambda$, $\kappa_\alpha + 1 = \kappa_\alpha$, so the hypothesis simplifies to a "pure" stepping-down lemma: $$2^\lambda \to (\kappa_\alpha)_{\alpha<\gamma}^{r+1} \implies \lambda \to (\kappa_\alpha)_{\alpha<\gamma}^r.$$ The condition $\kappa_\alpha \leq \lambda$ is needed to avoid a size obstruction: without it, the conclusion would require a subset of $\lambda$ of size $\kappa_\alpha > \lambda$, which is impossible (see `infinite_targets_needs_bound`).
  • r_eq_two research open AMS 5
    **$r = 2$ case.** The stepping-down from 3-uniform to 2-uniform partition relations: $2^\lambda \to (\kappa_\alpha + 1)_{\alpha<\gamma}^3$ implies $\lambda \to (\kappa_\alpha)_{\alpha<\gamma}^2$. Generalises the classical Erdős–Rado stepping-up/down theorem for pairs.
  • cardinalPartitionRel_one API AMS 5
    The partition relation $\mu \to (\nu)^r_1$ with a single color is equivalent to $\nu \le \mu$.
  • erdos_1167.unrestricted_is_false test AMS 5
    The unrestricted version of Erdős Problem 1167 (without the condition $\gamma \geq 2$ from the original Erdős–Hajnal list) is false. Taking $\gamma = 1$, $\kappa_0 = \aleph_1$, $\lambda = \aleph_0$: the premise $2^{\aleph_0} \to (\aleph_1 + 1)^3_1$ holds since $2^{\aleph_0} \geq \aleph_1$, but the conclusion $\aleph_0 \to (\aleph_1)^2_1$ fails since $\aleph_0 < \aleph_1$.
  • erdos_1167.variants.infinite_targets_needs_bound test AMS 5
    The `infinite_targets` variant without the bound $\kappa_\alpha \leq \lambda$ is false. Taking $\gamma = 1$, $\kappa_0 = 2^{\aleph_0}$, $\lambda = \aleph_0$: the premise $2^{\aleph_0} \to (2^{\aleph_0})^3_1$ holds since $2^{\aleph_0} \leq 2^{\aleph_0}$, but the conclusion $\aleph_0 \to (2^{\aleph_0})^2_1$ fails by Cantor's theorem.

    **Shelah's consistency result**: it is consistent with ZFC that there exists a graph $G$ with chromatic number $\aleph_1$ such that every triangle-free subgraph of $G$ has chromatic number strictly less than $\aleph_1$. Lean operates inside a single (fixed) model of its set theory, so we cannot directly express "consistent with ZFC" without leaving ZFC. Rather than pretend…

 Let $z_i$ be an infinite sequence of complex numbers such that $\lvert z_i\rvert=1$ for all $i\geq 1$, and for $n\geq 1$ let\[p_n(z)=\prod_{i\leq n} (z-z_i).\]Let $M_n=\max_{\lvert z\rvert=1}\lvert p_n(z)\rvert$. Is it true that $\limsup M_n=\infty$?Is it true that there exists $c>0$ such that for infinitely many $n$ we have $M_n > n^c$?Is it true that there exists $c>0$ such that, for all large $n$,\[\sum_{k\leq n}M_k > n^{1+c}?\]
3 Lean statements: 3 research solved
  • erdos_119.parts.i research solved AMS 30
    Is it true that $\limsup M_n = \infty$? This is Problem 4.1 in [Ha74] where it is attributed to Erdős. The weaker conjecture that $\limsup M_n=\infty$ was proved by Wagner [Wa80], who show that there is some $c>0$ with $M_n>(\log n)^c$ infinitely often.
  • erdos_119.parts.ii research solved AMS 30
    Is it true that there exists $c > 0$ such that for infinitely many $n$ we have $M_n > n^c$? The second question was answered by Beck [Be91], who proved that there exists some $c>0$ such that $\max_{n\leq N} M_n > N^c$.
  • erdos_119.parts.iii research solved AMS 30
    Is it true that there exists $c > 0$ such that, for all large $n$, $\sum_{k \leq n} M_k > n^{1 + c}$? The \$100 prize was offered for the third question in [Er97f]. This was resolved by GPT 5.6 and Korsky (see the proof claims), who proved that $\sum_{k\leq n}M_k \gg \frac{n^{5/4}}{\sqrt{\log n}}$ (and hence for infinitely many $n$ we have $M_n> n^{1/4-o(1)}$).

6 Lean statements: 3 research open, 3 research solved
  • erdos_1209.parts.i research solved AMS 11
    Let $A=\{a_1<a_2<\cdots\}$ be a sequence of integers which tends to infinity sufficiently fast. If there is an $n$ such that all $n+a_k$ are primes then must there exist infinitely many such $n$? Erdős [Er80] wrote 'unless I overlook a trivial way of getting a counterexample these questions are quite hopeless'. There is indeed a trivial counterexample (a variant of the construction in [erdosproblems.com/429]): define $a_1=2$ and for $k\geq 2$ let $a_k>a_{k-1}$ be a prime such that $a_k+k\equiv 0\pmod{q_k}$, where $q_k$ is some prime not dividing $k$. This sequence can be made to grow arbitrarily fast See also [erdosproblems.com/429] and [erdosproblems.com/1102].
  • erdos_1209.parts.ii research solved AMS 11
    What if we ask for $n+a_k$ to be squarefree instead of prime? A similar construction provides a counterexample to the squarefree question.
  • erdos_1209.parts.iii.a research solved AMS 11 · Lean proof
    Are there $n$ such that $n+2^{2^k}$ is always a prime? ebarschkis and GPT have proved that there are no $n$ such that $n+2^{2^k}$ is always prime: let $n\geq 3$ be any odd integer. If $k$ is chosen sufficiently large, and $p=n+2^{2^{k}}$ is prime, then the multiplicative order of $2^{2^k}\pmod{p}$, say $m$ is odd, and hence if $l$ is chosen such that $2^l\equiv 1\pmod{m}$ then $p\mid n+2^{2^{k+rl}}$ for all $r\geq 1$. This was formalized in Lean by Barschkis using ChatGPT.

    Let $G$ be the graph with vertex set those pairs $(x,y)\in \mathbb{N}^2$ with $\mathrm{gcd}(x,y)=1$, in which we join two vertices if the differ in only one coordinate, and there by $\pm 1$. Is there a path going to infinity on $G$, say $P$, such that for all $(x,y)\in P$ both $\min(x,y)>1$ and at least one of $x$ or $y$ is composite? The weaker version (only $\min(x,y) > 1$) was solved by C. Stewart via the prime-pair path $(p_k, p_{k+1}) \to (p_{k+1}, p_{k+2})$, as recounted in [Er80]; the compositeness condition forbids those anchors and the question is open.
  • vertical_leg_valid API AMS 11
    Core of the composite-anchor reduction: vertical-leg vertices $(a, s)$ for $b \le s \le c$ are valid vertices of the strengthened problem, given the anchor $a$ is composite and coprime to the whole leg.
  • horizontal_leg_valid API AMS 11
    Core of the composite-anchor reduction: horizontal-leg vertices $(s, c)$ for $a \le s \le b$ are valid, given the anchor $c$ is composite and coprime to the whole leg.
  • anchor_coprime_of_short_leg API AMS 11
    Roughness criterion (sufficiency for the anchor conditions): if $a < s$ for all $s$ in the leg and the leg stays below $a + P^-(a)$, then $a$ is coprime to the whole leg. Stated via divisibility: no prime factor of $a$ divides any $s$ with $a < s < a + p$ for all prime factors $p$ of $a$.
  • right_neighbor_witness_free API AMS 11
    Isolation lemma, right neighbour (core of the no-periodic-certificate theorem): if every prime in $P$ divides $x$ and none divides $y$, then no prime of $P$ divides either coordinate of $(x+1, y)$.
  • left_neighbor_witness_free API AMS 11
    Isolation lemma, left neighbour.
  • vertical_neighbor_both_even API AMS 11
    Isolation lemma, vertical neighbours: both coordinates even.

4 Lean statements: 1 research open, 3 research solved
  • erdos_123 research solved AMS 11 · Lean proof
    Let $a, b, c$ be three integers which are pairwise coprime. Is every large integer the sum of distinct integers of the form $a^k b^l c^m$ ($k, l, m ≥ 0$), none of which divide any other? Equivalently: is the set $\{a^k b^l c^m : k, l, m \geq 0\}$ d-complete? Note: For this not to reduce to the two-integer case, we need the integers to be greater than one and distinct. The prize of \$250 is offered by Erdős in [Er97] and [Er97e] for a 'proof or disproof'. The main problem was resolved in the affirmative by GPT 5.6 (prompted by Snyder). This was formalized in Lean by Alexeev.
  • erdos_123.variants.erdos_lewin_3_5_7 research solved AMS 11
    Erdős and Lewin [ErLe96] proved this conjecture when $a = 3$, $b = 5$, and $c = 7$.
  • erdos_123.variants.powers_2_3 research solved AMS 11
    A simpler case: the set of numbers of the form $2^k 3^l$ ($k, l ≥ 0$) is d-complete. This was initially conjectured by Erdős in 1992, who called it a "nice and difficult" problem, but it was quickly proven by Jansen and others using a simple inductive argument: - If $n = 2m$ is even, apply the inductive hypothesis to $m$ and double all summands. - If $n$ is odd, let $3^k$ be the largest power of $3$ with $3^k ≤ n$, and apply the inductive hypothesis to $n - 3^k$ (which is even).
  • erdos_123.variants.powers_2_3_5_snug research open AMS 11
    In [Er92b] Erdős makes the stronger conjecture (for $a=2$, $b=3$, and $c=5$) that, for any $\epsilon>0$, all large integers $n$ can be written as the sum of distinct integers $b_1<\cdots <b_t$ of the form $2^k3^l5^m$ where $b_t<(1+\epsilon)b_1$.

If we further have $\mathrm{gcd}(d_1,\ldots,d_r)=1$ then, for any $k\geq 1$, can all sufficiently large integers be written as a sum of the shape $\sum_i c_ia_i$ where $c_i\in \{0,1\}$ and $a_i\in P(d_i,k)$?

How large can the chromatic number and clique number of this graph be? In particular, can the chromatic number be infinite? How large the *clique* number can be is not addressed here.

    A minimal cut of a graph is a minimal set of vertices whose removal disconnects the graph. Let $c(n)$ be the maximum number of minimal cuts a graph on $n$ vertices can have. Does $c(n)^{1/n}\to \alpha$ for some $\alpha <2$? It is unclear in [Er88] whether Erdős knew that the limit existed, which follows from a simple argument first given in the literature (to the best of my knowledge) by Bradač [Br24]. That $\alpha<2$ was proved by Fomin, Kratsch, Todinca, and Villanger [FKTV08], who proved $\alpha \leq 1.7087$. Let $A\subset \{1,\ldots,N\}$ be a Sidon set with $\lvert A\rvert\sim N^{1/2}$. Must $A+A$ be well-distributed over all small moduli? In particular, must about half the elements of $A+A$ be even and half odd?

  • erdos_154 research solved AMS 5 AMS 11 · Lean proof
    Let $A\subset \{1,\ldots,N\}$ be a Sidon set with $\lvert A\rvert\sim N^{1/2}$. Must $A+A$ be well-distributed over all small moduli? In particular, must about half the elements of $A+A$ be even and half odd? The answer is yes. Lindström [Li98] proved the analogous statement for $A$ itself (see `erdos_154.variants.lindstrom`), later strengthened by Kolountzakis [Ko99]; well-distribution of $A+A$ then follows using the Sidon property. We state the question for the sumset: for any sequence of Sidon sets $A_k\subseteq\{0,\ldots,N_k\}$ with $N_k\to\infty$ and $\lvert A_k\rvert\sim N_k^{1/2}$, and any modulus $m\geq 2$, the proportion of elements of $A_k+A_k$ congruent to $i\pmod m$ (i.e. the co…
  • erdos_154.variants.lindstrom research solved AMS 5 AMS 11 · Lean proof
    Lindström's result for $A$ itself [Li98], later strengthened by Kolountzakis [Ko99]: for any sequence of Sidon sets $A_k\subseteq\{0,\ldots,N_k\}$ with $N_k\to\infty$ and $\lvert A_k\rvert\sim N_k^{1/2}$, and any modulus $m\geq 2$, the number of elements of $A_k$ congruent to $i\pmod m$, divided by $N_k^{1/2}$, tends to $1/m$ for every residue $i<m$. Well-distribution of $A+A$ (the actual question, `erdos_154`) follows from this using the Sidon property.

 We call $m$ practical if every integer $1\leq n<m$ is the sum of distinct divisors of $m$. If $m$ is practical then let $h(m)$ be such that $h(m)$ many divisors always suffice.Are there infinitely many practical $m$ such that\[h(m) < (\log\log m)^{O(1)}?\]Is it true that $h(n!)<n^{o(1)}$? Or perhaps even $h(n!)<(\log n)^{O(1)}$?
11 Lean statements: 3 research open, 2 research solved, 5 test, 1 textbook
  • practicalH_one test AMS 11
    $h(1) = 1$: we need the single divisor {1} to represent 1.
  • practicalH_two test AMS 11
    $h(2) = 1$: divisors are {1, 2}, each of m=1,2 needs only 1 divisor.
  • practicalH_six test AMS 11
    $h(6) = 2$: divisors are {1, 2, 3, 6}. The hardest m to represent is m=4 or m=5, each requiring 2 divisors: 4=1+3, 5=2+3.
  • practicalH_twelve test AMS 11
    $h(12) = 3$: divisors are {1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12}. The hardest m is m=11, requiring 3 divisors: 11=1+4+6.
  • practicalH_le_divisors test AMS 11
    For any practical number $n$, $h(n)$ ≤ number of divisors of $n$.
  • factorial_isPractical textbook AMS 11
    $h(n!)$ is well-defined since $n!$ is practical for $n ≥ 1$.
  • erdos_18a research open AMS 11
    **Conjecture 1.** Are there infinitely many practical numbers $m$ such that $h(m) < (\log \log m)^{O(1)}$? More precisely: does there exist a constant $C > 0$ such that for infinitely many practical numbers $m$, we have $h(m) < (\log \log m)^C$?
  • erdos_18b research open AMS 11
    **Conjecture 2.** Is it true that $h(n!) < n^{o(1)}$? That is, for all $\varepsilon > 0$, is $h(n!) < n^\varepsilon$ for sufficiently large $n$?
  • erdos_18c research open AMS 11
    **Conjecture 3.** Or perhaps even $h(n!) < (\log n)^{O(1)}$? Erdős offered \$250 for a proof or disproof.
  • erdos_18_upper_bound research solved AMS 11
    **Erdős's Theorem.** Erdős proved that $h(n!) < n$ for all $n \ge 1$.
  • erdos_18_vose research solved AMS 11
    **Vose's Theorem.** Vose proved the existence of infinitely many practical numbers $m$ such that $h(m) \ll (\log m)^{1/2}$. This gives a positive answer to a weaker form of Conjecture 1.

    Let $n_1<\cdots < n_r\leq N$ with associated $a_i\pmod{n_i}$ such that the congruence classes are disjoint (that is, every integer is $\equiv a_i\pmod{n_i}$ for at most one $1\leq i\leq r$). How large can $r$ be in terms of $N$? Let $f(N)$ be the maximum possible $r$, and let $L(N)=\exp(\sqrt{\log N\log\log N})$. This was proved by GPT-5.4 Pro (prompted by Ho Boon Suan), using the argument of [BFV13] together with the resolution of the Kahn-Kalai conjecture by Park and Pham [PaPh24], so that $$f(N)= N L(N)^{-1+o(1)}.$$

    Are there $n$ such that there is a covering system with moduli the divisors of $n$ which is 'as disjoint as possible'? That is, for all $d\mid n$ with $d>1$ there is an associated $a_d$ such that every integer is congruent to some $a_d\pmod{d}$, and if there is some integer $x$ with $$x\equiv a_d\pmod{d}\textrm{ and }x\equiv a_{d'}\pmod{d'}$$then $(d,d')=1$.   • erdos_205.parts.i research solved AMS 11
    Is it true that all sufficiently large $n$ can be written as $2^k+m$ for some $k\geq 0$, where $\Omega(m)<\log\log m$? (Here $\Omega(m)$ is the number of prime divisors of $m$ counted with multiplicity.) Barreto and Leeham, using ChatGPT and Aristotle, have proved a negative answer, which was quantified by Tao and Alexeev (see the comments): in fact there are infinitely many $n$ such that, for all $k$ with $2^k<n$, $n-2^k$ has at least $$\gg \left(\frac{\log n}{\log\log n}\right)^{1/2}$$ many prime factors.

    Let $x>0$ be a real number. For any $n\geq 1$ let $$R_n(x) = \sum_{i=1}^n\frac{1}{m_i}<x$$ be the maximal sum of $n$ distinct unit fractions which is $<x$. Is it true that, for almost all $x$, for sufficiently large $n$, we have $$R_{n+1}(x)=R_n(x)+\frac{1}{m},$$ where $m$ is minimal such that $m$ does not appear in $R_n(x)$ and the right-hand side is $<x$? (That is, are the best underapproximations eventually always constructed in a 'greedy' fashion?) Kovač [Ko24b] has proved that this is false - in fact as false as possible: the set of $x\in (0,\infty)$ for which the best underapproximations are eventually 'greedy' has Lebesgue measure zero.

6 Lean statements: 6 research solved
  • erdos_214 research solved AMS 5 AMS 52 · Lean proof
    Let $S\subset \mathbb{R}^2$ be such that no two points in $S$ are distance $1$ apart. Must the complement of $S$ contain four points which form a unit square? The answer is yes, proved by Juhász [Ju79], who proved more generally that the complement of $S$ must contain a congruent copy of any set of four points.
  • erdos_214.variants.juhasz research solved AMS 5 AMS 52
    The answer is yes, proved by Juhász [Ju79], who proved more generally that the complement of $S$ must contain a congruent copy of any set of four points.

Let $\epsilon>0$ and $n$ be sufficiently large depending on $\epsilon$. Is there a graph on $n$ vertices with $\geq n^2/8$ many edges which contains no $K_4$ such that the largest independent set has size at most $\epsilon n$?
5 Lean statements: 4 research solved, 1 test
  • erdos_22 research solved AMS 5
    Let $\epsilon > 0$ and let $n$ be sufficiently large depending on $\epsilon$. Is there a graph on $n$ vertices with at least $n^2/8$ many edges which contains no $K_4$, such that the largest independent set has size at most $\epsilon n$? This is true, as proved by Fox, Loh, and Zhao [FLZ15].
  • erdos_22.variants.szemeredi_upper research solved AMS 5
    The matching upper bound, due to Szemerédi [Sz72]: a $K_4$-free graph on $n$ vertices whose independence number is sublinear in $n$ has at most $(1/8 + o(1))n^2$ edges. That is, for every $\epsilon > 0$ there is a $\delta > 0$ such that for all sufficiently large $n$, every $K_4$-free graph $G$ on $n$ vertices with $\alpha(G) \leq \delta n$ has at most $(1/8 + \epsilon)n^2$ edges.
  • erdos_22.variants.bollobas_erdos_lower research solved AMS 5
    The construction of Bollobás and Erdős [BoEr76]: for every $\epsilon > 0$ and $\delta > 0$, for all sufficiently large $n$ there is a $K_4$-free graph on $n$ vertices with independence number at most $\delta n$ and at least $(1/8 - \epsilon)n^2$ edges. Together with `erdos_22.variants.szemeredi_upper` this shows that the Ramsey–Turán density of $K_4$ is $1/8$.
  • erdos_22.variants.fox_loh_zhao research solved AMS 5
    The quantitative strengthening proved by Fox, Loh, and Zhao [FLZ15]: there is a constant $C > 0$ such that for all sufficiently large $n$ there exists a $K_4$-free graph on $n$ vertices with at least $n^2/8$ edges whose largest independent set has size at most $$C \cdot \frac{(\log\log n)^{3/2}}{(\log n)^{1/2}} \cdot n.$$
  • erdos_22.variants.test_bot test AMS 5
    A sanity check for `erdos_22.variants.szemeredi_upper`: the empty graph is $K_4$-free and trivially satisfies the upper bound $(1/8 + \epsilon)n^2$ on the number of edges.

    		 Let $f(N)$ be the maximum size of $A\subseteq \{1,\ldots,N\}$ such that the sums $a+b+c$ with $a,b,c\in A$ are all distinct (aside from the trivial coincidences). Is it true that\[ f(N)\sim N^{1/3}?\]
    5 Lean statements: 2 research open, 3 research solved
    • erdos_241 research open AMS 5
      Is it true that $f(N)\sim N^{1/3}$? Originally asked to Erdős by Bose. This is discussed in problem C11 of Guy's collection [Gu04].
    • erdos_241.variants.lower_bound research solved AMS 5
      Bose and Chowla [BoCh62] provided a construction proving one half of this, namely $(1+o(1))N^{1/3}\leq f(N)$.
    • erdos_241.variants.upper_bound research solved AMS 5
      The best upper bound known to date is due to Green [Gr01], $f(N) \leq ((7/2)^{1/3}+o(1))N^{1/3}$. (note that $(7/2)^{1/3}\approx 1.519$).
    • erdos_241.variants.generalization research open AMS 5
      More generally, Bose and Chowla [BoCh62] conjectured that the maximum size of $A\subseteq \{1,\ldots,N\}$ with all $r$-fold sums distinct (aside from the trivial coincidences) then $\lvert A\rvert \sim N^{1/r}.$
    • erdos_241.variants.r_eq_2 research solved AMS 5
      This is known only for $r=2$ (see [erdosproblems.com/30]).

    		 Are there infinitely many $n$ such that there exists some $t\geq 2$ and distinct integers $a_1,\ldots,a_t\geq 1$ such that\[\frac{n}{2^n}=\sum_{1\leq k\leq t}\frac{a_k}{2^{a_k}}?\]Is this true for all $n$? Is there a rational $x$ such that\[x = \sum_{k=1}^\infty \frac{a_k}{2^{a_k}}\]has at least $2^{\aleph_0}$ solutions?
    7 Lean statements: 3 research open, 2 research solved, 2 textbook
    • erdos_261.variants.borwein_loring textbook AMS 11
      For every positive integer $m$, if $n = 2^{m+1} - m - 2$, then $$\frac{n}{2^n} = \sum_{n < k \le n + m} \frac{k}{2^k}.$$ This construction is due to Borwein and Loring [BoLo90].
    • erdos_261.variants.borwein_loring_property textbook AMS 11
      The Borwein--Loring construction gives the required property when $m \ge 2$. This lower bound ensures that the representation contains at least two terms.
    • erdos_261.parts.i research solved AMS 11
      Are there infinitely many positive integers $n$ such that there exist some $t \ge 2$ and distinct integers $a_1, \ldots, a_t \ge 1$ satisfying $$\frac{n}{2^n} = \sum_{1 \le k \le t} \frac{a_k}{2^{a_k}}?$$ In [Er88c], Erdős notes that Cusick had a simple proof that infinitely many such $n$ exist.
    • erdos_261.variants.le_10000 research solved AMS 11
      Tengely, Ulas, and Zygadlo [TUZ20] verified that every positive integer $n \le 10000$ has the required property.
    • erdos_261.parts.ii research open AMS 11
      Do all positive integers $n$ have the required property?
    • erdos_261.parts.iii research open AMS 11
      Is there a rational number $x$ such that $$x = \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \frac{a_k}{2^{a_k}}$$ has at least $2^{\aleph_0}$ representations by pairwise distinct positive integers $a_k$?
    • erdos_261.variants.two_representations research open AMS 11
      In [Er88c], Erdős asks the weaker question of whether there exists a rational $x$ with at least two representations $$x = \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \frac{a_k}{2^{a_k}}$$ by pairwise distinct positive integers $a_k$.

    		 Let $a_n$ be an increasing sequence of positive integers such that for every sequence of positive integers $b_n$ with $b_n/a_n\to 1$ the sum\[\sum\frac{1}{b_n}\]is irrational. Is $a_n=2^{2^n}$ such a sequence? Must such a sequence satisfy $a_n^{1/n}\to \infty$?
    6 Lean statements: 2 research open, 4 research solved
    • erdos_263.parts.i research open AMS 11
      Is $a_n = 2^{2^n}$ an irrationality sequence in the above sense?
    • erdos_263.parts.ii research open AMS 11
      Must every irrationality sequence $a_n$ in the above sense satisfy $a_n^{1/n} \to \infty$ as $n \to \infty$? Note: this was answered **false** for the *pre-correction* statement, which did not require monotonicity — the counterexample sequence is not increasing. The problem was corrected on erdosproblems.com on 2026-04-02 to require increasing sequences; for the corrected statement this question is **open**. The earlier formal proof (for the pre-correction definition) is preserved at https://github.com/google-deepmind/formal-conjectures/blob/c8cf651906abe91051cf835d4232ad5648412113/FormalConjectures/ErdosProblems/263.lean#L298
    • erdos_263.variants.folklore research solved AMS 11
      A folklore result states that any $a_n$ satisfying $\lim_{n \to \infty} a_n^{\frac{1}{2^n}} = \infty$ has $\sum \frac{1}{a_n}$ converging to an irrational number.
    • erdos_263.variants.sub_doubly_exponential research solved AMS 11
      Kovač and Tao [KoTa24] proved that any strictly increasing sequence $a_n$ such that $\sum \frac{1}{a_n}$ converges and $\lim \frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n^2} = 0$ is not an irrationality sequence in the above sense. [KoTa24] Kovač, V. and Tao T., On several irrationality problems for Ahmes series. arXiv:2406.17593 (2024).
    • erdos_263.variants.super_doubly_exponential research solved AMS 11 · Lean proof
      On the other hand, if there exists some $\varepsilon > 0$ such that $a_n$ satisfies $\liminf \frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n^{2+\varepsilon}} > 0$, then $a_n$ is an irrationality sequence by the above folklore result `erdos_263.variants.folklore`.
    • erdos_263.variants.doubly_exponential_all_but_countable research solved AMS 11
      Koizumi [Ko25] showed that $a_n = \lfloor \alpha^{2^n} \rfloor$ is an irrationality sequence for all but countably many $\alpha > 1$. [Ko25] Koizumi, J., Irrationality of the reciprocal sum of doubly exponential sequences, arXiv:2504.05933 (2025).

    • erdos_275 research solved AMS 11 · Lean proof
      If a finite system of $r$ congruences $\{ a_i\pmod{n_i} : 1\leq i\leq r\}$ (the $n_i$ are not necessarily distinct) covers $2^r$ consecutive integers then it covers all integers. This is best possible as the system $2^{i-1}\pmod{2^i}$ shows. This was proved independently by Selfridge and Crittenden and Vanden Eynden [CrVE70]. This was formalized in Lean by Alexeev using Aristotle.

    		Let $A\subseteq \mathbb{N}$ be an infinite set and consider the following greedy algorithm for a rational $x\in (0,1)$: choose the minimal $n\in A$ such that $n\geq 1/x$ and repeat with $x$ replaced by $x-\frac{1}{n}$. If this terminates after finitely many steps then this produces a representation of $x$ as the sum of distinct unit fractions with denominators from $A$.Does this process always terminate if $x$ has odd denominator and $A$ is the set of odd numbers? More generally, for which pairs $x$ and $A$ does this process terminate?

      Let $A\subseteq \mathbb{N}$ be an infinite set and consider the following greedy algorithm for a rational $x\in (0,1)$: choose the minimal $n\in A$ such that $n\geq 1/x$ and repeat with $x$ replaced by $x-\frac{1}{n}$. If this terminates after finitely many steps then this produces a representation of $x$ as the sum of distinct unit fractions with denominators from $A$. Does this process always terminate if $x$ has odd denominator and $A$ is the set of odd numbers?
    • erdos_282.variants.general research open AMS 5 · value-typed
      More generally, for which pairs $x$ and $A$ does this process terminate?
    • erdos_282.variants.fibonacci textbook AMS 5
      In 1202 Fibonacci observed that this process terminates for any $x$ when $A=\mathbb{N}$.
    • erdos_282.variants.graham research open AMS 5
      Graham has shown that $\frac{m}{n}$ is the sum of distinct unit fractions with denominators $\equiv a\pmod{d}$ if and only if $$\left(\frac{n}{(n,a,d)},\frac{d}{(a,d)}\right)=1.$$ Does the greedy algorithm always terminate in such cases?
    • greedyUnitFractionRem_sq_one test AMS 5
    • erdos_282.variants.sq research open AMS 5
      Graham has also shown that $x$ is the sum of distinct unit fractions with square denominators if and only if $x\in [0,\pi^2/6-1)\cup [1,\pi^2/6)$. Does the greedy algorithm for this always terminate? Erdős and Graham believe not - indeed, perhaps it fails to terminate almost always.

    		 Let $p:\mathbb{Z}\to \mathbb{Z}$ be a polynomial whose leading coefficient is positive and such that there exists no $d\geq 2$ with $d\mid p(n)$ for all $n\geq 1$. Is it true that, for all sufficiently large $m$, there exist integers $1\leq n_1<\cdots <n_k$ such that\[1=\frac{1}{n_1}+\cdots+\frac{1}{n_k}\]and\[m=p(n_1)+\cdots+p(n_k)?\]
    8 Lean statements: 8 research solved
    • erdos_283 research solved AMS 11 · Lean proof
      Let $p\colon \mathbb{Z} \rightarrow \mathbb{Z}$ be a polynomial whose leading coefficient is positive and such that there exists no $d≥2$ with $d ∣ p(n)$ for all $n≥1$. Is it true that, for all sufficiently large $m$, there exist integers $1≤n_1<\dots < n_k$ such that $$1=\frac{1}{n_1}+\cdots+\frac{1}{n_k}$$ and $$m=p(n_1)+\cdots+p(n_k)$$? GPT 5.5 Pro (prompted by Price) has given a proof that the answer is yes, for the stronger version with $1$ replaced by any rational $\alpha>0$. This was formalized in Lean by Ammanamanchi using Opus 4.6 and GPT 5.5 Pro.
    • erdos_283.variants.graham research solved AMS 11
      Graham [Gr63] has proved this when $p(x)=x$.
    • erdos_283.variants.graham_alpha research solved AMS 11
      Graham also conjectures that this remains true with $1$ replaced by an arbitrary rational $\alpha>0$ (provided $m$ is taken sufficiently large depending on $\alpha$).
    • erdos_283.variants.cassels research solved AMS 11
      Cassels [Ca60] has proved that these conditions on the polynomial imply every sufficiently large integer is the sum of $p(n_i)$ with distinct $n_i$.
    • erdos_283.variants.burr research solved AMS 11
      Burr has proved this if $p(x)=x^k$ with $k\geq 1$ and if we allow $n_i=n_j$.
    • erdos_283.variants.alekseyev research solved AMS 11
      Alekseyev [Al19] has proved this when $p(x)=x^2$, for all $m>8542$.
    • erdos_283.variants.van_doorn_linear research solved AMS 11
      van Doorn [vD25] has investigated the question of what 'sufficiently large' means for $p(x)=x$. van Doorn has also proved the original conjecture for many linear and quadratic polynomials. For example, if $p(x) = x + b$ with $1 \leq b \leq 5000$, then the conjecture is true.
    • erdos_283.variants.van_doorn_quadratic research solved AMS 11
      van Doorn [vD25] has proved the original conjecture for many linear and quadratic polynomials. For example, if $p(x) = x^2 + b$ with $1 \leq b \leq 800$, then the conjecture is true.

      The lower bound of $\geq 2$ is equivalent to saying that $1$ is not the sum of reciprocals of consecutive integers, proved by Erdős [Er32].
    • erdos_287.test.best_possible test AMS 11

    • erdos_287.variants.prime_conjecture research open AMS 11
      For all large $N$, there exists a prime $p \in [N, 2N]$ such that $\frac{p+1}{2}$ is also prime. This is an open conjecture. If true, it would imply `erdos_287` for all but at most finitely many exceptions (see `erdos_287.variants.prime_conjecture_implies`).
    • erdos_287.variants.prime_conjecture_implies textbook AMS 11
      The conjecture `erdos_287` would follow for all but at most finitely many exceptions if it were known that, for all large $N$, there exists a prime $p \in [N, 2N]$ such that $\frac{p+1}{2}$ is also prime. More precisely: if the prime conjecture holds, then there exists $k_0$ such that for all $k \geq k_0$, any Egyptian fraction representation of $1$ with $k$ terms and all terms $> 1$ must have $\max(n_{i+1} - n_i) \geq 3$.

    • erdos_290 research solved AMS 11 · Lean proof
      Let $a\geq 1$. Must there exist some $b>a$ such that $$\sum_{a\leq n\leq b}\frac{1}{n}=\frac{r_1}{s_1}\textrm{ and } \sum_{a\leq n\leq b+1}\frac{1}{n}=\frac{r_2}{s_2},$$ with $(r_i,s_i)=1$ and $s_2<s_1$? If so, how does this $b(a)$ grow with $a$? This was resolved in the affirmative by van Doorn [vD24], who proved $b=b(a)$ always exists, and in fact $b(a) \ll a$. Indeed, if $a\in (3^k,3^{k+1}]$ then one can take $b=2\cdot 3^{k+1}-1$. van Doorn also proves that $b(a)>a+(1/2-o(1))\log a$, and considers various generalisations of the original problem.

    8 Lean statements: 3 research open, 3 research solved, 2 test
    • L_eval test AMS 11
    • a_eval test AMS 11
    • erdos_291.parts.i research open AMS 11
      Let $n\geq 1$ and define $L_n$ to be the least common multiple of $\{1,\ldots,n\}$ and $a_n$ by $\sum_{1\leq k\leq n}\frac{1}{k}=\frac{a_n}{L_n}$. Is it true that $(a_n,L_n)=1$ occurs for infinitely many $n$?
    • erdos_291.parts.ii research solved AMS 11
      Is it true that $(a_n,L_n)>1$ occurs for infinitely many $n$? Steinerberger has observed that the answer to the second question is trivially yes: for example, any $n$ which begins with a $2$ in base $3$ has $3\mid (a_n,L_n)$.
    • erdos_291.variants.steinerberger_generalization research solved AMS 11
      More generally, if the leading digit of $n$ in base $p$ is $p-1$ then $p\mid (a_n,L_n)$. There is in fact a necessary and sufficient condition: a prime $p\leq n$ divides $(a_n,L_n)$ if and only if $p$ divides the numerator of $1+\cdots+\frac{1}{k}$, where $k$ is the leading digit of $n$ in base $p$. This can be seen by writing $a_n = \frac{L_n}{1}+\cdots+\frac{L_n}{n}$ and observing that the right-hand side is congruent to $1+\cdots+1/k$ modulo $p$. (The previous claim about $p-1$ follows immediately from Wolstenholme's theorem.)
    • erdos_291.variants.shiu_heuristic_asymptotic research open AMS 11
      This leads to a heuristic prediction (see for example a preprint of Shiu [Sh16]) of $\asymp\frac{x}{\log x}$ for the number of $n\in [1,x]$ such that $(a_n,L_n)=1$.
    • erdos_291.variants.shiu_heuristic_density_zero research open AMS 11
      In particular, there should be infinitely many $n$, but the set of such $n$ should have density zero. Unfortunately this heuristic is difficult to turn into a proof.
    • erdos_291.variants.wu_yan research solved AMS 11
      Wu and Yan [WuYa22] have proved, conditional on $\frac{1}{\log p}$ being linearly independent over $\mathbb{Q}$ for any finite collection of primes $p$ (itself a consequence of Schanuel's conjecture), that the set of $n$ for which $(a_n,L_n)>1$ has upper density $1$.

      A machine-checked **barrier** for Erdős 307 (Bonfioli, 2026): any solution with `Q` nonempty uses at least 59 primes in total, and `(∏_{p ∈ P} p)² ≥ 4·10¹¹²` — i.e. `∏_{p ∈ P} p ≥ 2·10⁵⁶` (and, by symmetry, the same for `∏ Q`); so no solution lies below a prime-product of `2.09·10⁵⁶`. The full `sorry`-free proof is in the linked repository (`Closed.lean`): the left conjunct is `card_ge_59`, the right is `erdos307_barrier_closed`. Both depend on `propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound` and nothing further: the evaluation of the first 59 primes is kernel-checked by `decide`, so no `native_decide` enters this statement.

    1 Lean statements: 1 research solved
    • erdos_314 research solved AMS 11 AMS 40 · Lean proof
      Let $n\geq 1$ and let $m$ be minimal such that $\sum_{n\leq k\leq m}\frac{1}{k}\geq 1$. We define $$\epsilon(n) = \sum_{n\leq k\leq m}\frac{1}{k}-1.$$ How small can $\epsilon(n)$ be? Is it true that $$\liminf n^2\epsilon(n)=0?$$ This is true, and shown by Lim and Steinerberger [LiSt24], who further proved that, for any $\delta>0$, there exist infinitely many $n$ and $m$ such that $$n^2\left\lvert \sum_{n\leq k\leq m}\frac{1}{k}-1\right\rvert\ll \frac{1}{(\log n)^{5/4-\delta}}.$$ Erdős and Graham (and also Lim and Steinerberger) believe that the exponent of $2$ is best possible here, in that $\liminf \epsilon(n) n^{2+\delta}=\infty$ for all $\delta>0$.

    • erdos_315 research solved AMS 11 · Lean proof
      Let $u_1=1$ and $u_{n+1}=u_n(u_n+1)$, so that $\sum_{k\geq 1}\frac{1}{u_k+1}$ and $u_k=\lfloor c_0^{2^k}+1\rfloor$ for $k\geq 1$, where $$c_0=\lim u_n^{1/2^n}=1.264085\cdots.$$ Let $a_1<a_2<\cdots $ be any other sequence with $\sum \frac{1}{a_k}=1$. Is it true that $$\liminf a_n^{1/2^n}<c_0=1.264085\cdots?$$ This is true, and was proved independently by Kamio [Ka25] and Li and Tang [LiTa25]. An earlier interpretation of this question on this site defined $u_1=2$ and $u_{n+1}=u_n^2-u_n+1$ (Sylvester's sequence), which is the same sequence shifted by $1$; we use the phrasing above as more faithful to [ErGr80]. The constant $c_0$ is called the Vardi constant.

      Is it true that if $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}\setminus\{1\}$ is a finite set with $\sum_{n \in A} \frac{1}{n} < 2$ then there is a partition $A=A_1 \sqcup A_2$ such that $\sum_{n \in A_i} \frac{1}{n} < 1$ for $i=1,2$?       Let $R(N)$ be the maximal such size. Results of Bleicher and Erdős from [BlEr75] and [BlEr76b] imply that $$ \frac{N}{\log N} \prod_{i=3}^{k} \log_i N \le R(N), $$ valid for any $k \ge 4$ with $\log_k N \ge k$ and any $r \ge 1$ with $\log_{2r} N \ge 1$. (In these bounds $\log_i n$ denotes the $i$-fold iterated logarithm.) [BlEr75] Bleicher, M. N. and Erdős, P., _The number of distinct subsums of $\sum \sb{1}\spN\,1/i$_. Math. Comp. (1975), 29-42. [BlEr76b] Bleicher, Michael N. and Erdős, Paul, _Denominators of Egyptian fractions. II_. Illinois J. Math. (1976), 598-613.
    • erdos_321.variants.upper research solved AMS 11
      Let $R(N)$ be the maximal such size. Results of Bleicher and Erdős from [BlEr75] and [BlEr76b] imply that $$ R(N) \le \frac{1}{\log 2} \log_r N \left( \frac{N}{\log N} \prod_{i=3}^{r} \log_i N \right), $$ valid for any $k \ge 4$ with $\log_k N \ge k$ and any $r \ge 1$ with $\log_{2r} N \ge 1$. (In these bounds $\log_i n$ denotes the $i$-fold iterated logarithm.) [BlEr75] Bleicher, M. N. and Erdős, P., _The number of distinct subsums of $\sum \sb{1}\spN\,1/i$_. Math. Comp. (1975), 29-42. [BlEr76b] Bleicher, Michael N. and Erdős, Paul, _Denominators of Egyptian fractions. II_. Illinois J. Math. (1976), 598-613.

    • erdos_329.variants.converse_implication research open AMS 5 AMS 11
      The converse: if the maximum density is 1, then any finite Sidon set can be embedded in a perfect difference set modulo $n > 0$. Since the consequent is false (due to the counterexamples in [Ha47] and [AlMi25]), this implication is logically equivalent to the statement that the maximum upper density of Sidon sets is NOT 1. Because the maximum upper density problem is still open, the truth value of this implication is also an open research problem.

      Let $A\subseteq \mathbb{N}$ be a set of density zero. Does there exist a $B$ such that $A\subseteq B+B$ and $$\lvert B\cap \{1,\ldots,N\}\rvert =o(N^{1/2})$$ for all large $N$? The answer is no. Erdős and Newman [ErNe77] have proved this is true when $A$ is the set of squares. In fact, Theorem 2 of [ErNe77] already implies a negative answer to this problem, but this seems to have been overlooked by Erdős and Graham. See also [806].

      Let $A\subseteq \mathbb{N}$ be an additive basis (of any finite order) such that $\lvert A\cap \{1,\ldots,N\}\rvert=o(N)$. Is it true that $$ \lim_{N\to \infty}\frac{\lvert (A+A)\cap \{1,\ldots,N\}\rvert} {\lvert A\cap \{1,\ldots,N\}\rvert}=\infty? $$ The answer is no, and a counterexample was provided by Turjányi [Tu84]. This was generalised (to the replacement of $A+A$ by the $h$-fold sumset $hA$ for any $h\geq 2$) by Ruzsa and Turjányi [RT85]. "Additive basis" is `Set.IsAsymptoticAddBasis`: some finite $h$ has $hA$ containing every sufficiently large integer. The exact notion `Set.IsAddBasis`, which asks that $hA$ be all of $\mathbb{N}$, would force $0, 1 \in A$ and is not the class thes…

    • alpha_gt_two_not_isGoodPair research solved AMS 11 · Lean proof
      For $\alpha > 2$ and any $t > 0$, the sequence $\lfloor t\alpha^n\rfloor$ is not additively complete; equivalently $(t, \alpha)$ is not a "good pair". A partial result on the open Erdős Problem 349: it complements `complete_for_alpha_in_Ioo_one_to_goldenRatio`. The proof is recorded via the `formal_proof` mechanism rather than written inline, as it exceeds the repository's proof-length guideline.
    • alpha_le_one_not_isGoodPair research solved AMS 11 · Lean proof
      For $0 < \alpha \le 1$ and any $t > 0$, $(t, \alpha)$ is not a good pair: every term $\lfloor t\alpha^n\rfloor$ lies in the finite interval $[0, \lfloor t\rfloor]$ (since $\alpha^n \le 1$), so every subset sum is bounded by the constant $\sum_{i \in [0,\lfloor t\rfloor]} i$, and no large integer can be a subset sum. A partial result on the open Erdős Problem 349, complementing the $2 < \alpha$ and integer-coefficient cases.
    • exists_finsetSum_two_pow research solved AMS 11 · Lean proof
      **Binary expansion.** Every natural number $k$ is a sum of distinct powers of two: there is a finite set $E$ of exponents with $k = \sum_{i \in E} 2^i$. Proved by strong induction: subtract the largest power $2^m \le k$, recurse on the remainder.
    • one_two_isGoodPair research solved AMS 11 · Lean proof
      **The pair $(1, 2)$ is good.** The powers of two $\lfloor 1\cdot 2^n\rfloor = 2^n$ form an additively complete set: every $k \ge 1$ is a finite sum of distinct powers of two.
    • dyadic_two_isGoodPair research solved AMS 11 · Lean proof
      **The dyadic fiber at $\alpha = 2$.** For every $k$, the pair $(1/2^k, 2)$ is good: the sequence $\lfloor 2^n / 2^k\rfloor$ is additively complete because at index $n = m + k$ it equals the exact power $2^m$, so its range contains all powers of two, which already form an additively complete set. Uses monotonicity `IsAddComplete.mono`.
    • int_coeff_ge_two_not_isGoodPair research solved AMS 11 · Lean proof
      **Integer leading coefficient $t \ge 2$ blocks completeness.** For every integer base $\alpha$, the pair $(t, \alpha)$ with integer $t \ge 2$ is not good: $\lfloor t\alpha^n\rfloor = t\alpha^n$ is a multiple of $t$, so every subset sum is too, but two consecutive large integers cannot both be multiples of $t$. Generalizes the parity obstruction ($t = 2$). A partial result on Erdős Problem 349.
    • integer_isGoodPair_iff research solved AMS 11 · Lean proof
      **Erdős Problem 349, complete characterization on positive integer pairs.** For integers $t \ge 1$, $\alpha \ge 1$, the pair $(t, \alpha)$ is good (i.e. $\lfloor t\alpha^n\rfloor$ is additively complete) iff $(t, \alpha) = (1, 2)$. Assembles the four partial results: $(1,2)$ is good, $\alpha \le 1$ fails, $2 < \alpha$ fails (`alpha_gt_two_not_isGoodPair`), and integer $t \ge 2$ fails.

      If `A ⊂ ℕ` is a finite set of integers all of whose subset sums are distinct then `∑ n ∈ A, 1/n < 2`. Proved by Ryavec. This was proved by Ryavec, who did not appear to ever publish the proof. Ryavec's proof is reproduced in [BeEr74]. More generally, Ryavec's proof delivers that $\sum_{n\in A}\frac{1}{n}\leq 2-2^{1-\lvert A\rvert},$ with equality if and only if $A=\{1,2,\ldots,2^k\}$. This was formalized in Lean by Alexeev using Aristotle.

      If `A ⊂ ℕ` is a finite set of integers all of whose subset sums are distinct then `∑ n ∈ A, 1/n^s < 1/(1 - 2^(-s))`, for any `s > 0`. Proved by Hanson, Steele, and Stenger [HSS77]. We exclude here the case `s = 0`, because in the informal formulation then the right hand side is to be interpreted as `∞`, while the left hand side counts the elements in `A`.

      Is there a lacunary sequence $A\subseteq \mathbb{N}$ (so that $A=\{a_1 < \cdots\}$ and there exists some $\lambda > 1$ such that $a_{n+1}/a_n\geq \lambda$ for all $n\geq 1$) such that $$\left\{ \sum_{a\in A'}\frac{1}{a} : A'\subseteq A\textrm{ finite}\right\}$$ contain all rationals in some open interval? Bleicher and Erdős conjectured the answer is no. In fact the answer is yes, with any lacunarity constant $\lambda\in (1,2)$ (though not $\lambda=2$), as proved by van Doorn and Kova\v{c} [DoKo25]. This was formalized in Lean by van Doorn using Aristotle.
